source.title_on_document: The impact of AI-assisted composition tools on cultivating creativity among music students in Guangdong province

supplement.where: No supplementary material or appendix is referenced in the document; the PDF ends with transparency, copyright, and references on p. 25.
supplement.holds: No supplementary statistics or external appendix are identified.

paper_design_summary: Music students from four Guangdong institutions were assigned to a generative AI composition curriculum or traditional instruction, with 120 students analyzed, 60 per arm (PDF pp. 5-7 and 13-15). Explicit randomization claims support field_rct coding despite the conflicting quasi-experimental label; experts assessed produced compositions on nine dimensions and additional composites (PDF pp. 5-7 and 17-23). AI access during the main post-test production is unspecified, although Table 7's selected examples are expressly described as AI-assisted (PDF p. 18).

studies.label: Music composition curriculum in Guangdong institutions

assignment.what_was_assigned: Students were divided into the AI-assisted composition curriculum and traditional-instruction groups. Figure 1 labels the division Randomized Assignment and shows 60 students per arm. The sequence-generation method, concealment, and any institution-level blocking are not stated; the prose also calls the design quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: The randomization procedure was effective in creating comparable groups with similar distributions across gender, age, grade level, prior music experience, and primary instrument selection, ensuring valid comparison of intervention effects.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 2794), Figure 1, Group Division / Randomized Assignment and arm counts; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 2796), paragraph after Table 1 (quote). Educational setting and conflicting quasi-experimental label: PDF pp. 5-6, Sec. 3.1.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration or registration identifier is stated in the PDF; research methods are on PDF pp. 5-8.

arms.name: AI-assisted composition curriculum
arms.description: Composition instruction with the purpose-built generative AI-Assisted Composition Platform, including melody generation and modification, harmonic generation, structural integration, and culturally informed composition projects (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; p. 9, Table 2; pp. 11-12, Table 4). Assigned arm count: PDF p. 5, Figure 1; analyzed arm count: PDF pp. 13 and 15, Tables 5-6.

arms.name: Traditional composition instruction
arms.description: Traditional composition approaches and instruction during the same intervention period (PDF p. 5, Sec. 3.1 and Figure 1; p. 6, Sec. 3.1). No alternative generative AI tool is specified. Assigned arm count: PDF p. 5, Figure 1; analyzed arm count: PDF pp. 13 and 15, Tables 5-6.

participants.exclusions: No exclusion, attrition, or missing-outcome flow is reported. Figure 1 shows the recruitment/assignment sample and Tables 5-6 retain 60 students per arm; this is not taken as a claim of intention-to-treat analysis. A separate pilot of 28 music students is expressly outside the primary study and is not added to these counts (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2).
participants.who: Music students from four institutions offering specialised music programmes in Guangdong; Table 1 lists sophomore, junior, and senior students, age range 17-24 (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.3; p. 7, Table 1).
participants.quote: The primary source of information data was 120 music students from four institutions offering specialised music programmes in Guangdong Province.
participants.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 2795), Sec. 3.3 (quote and recruitment); PDF p. 5, Figure 1 (assignment: n=120, 60 per arm); PDF p. 7, Table 1 (people and demographics); PDF pp. 13 and 15, Tables 5-6 (60 analyzed per arm).

ai_tool.name_model: AI-Assisted Composition Platform (AICP), a purpose-built platform integrating generative artificial neural networks; specific architecture, model version, and vendor not stated (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2).
ai_tool.how_used: Interactive music generation and composition assistance: students generated and modified AI-suggested melodies, manipulated AI-generated harmonic progressions, and used form generation, arrangement assistance, and a full composition environment (PDF p. 9, Table 2). This is an educational composition platform rather than a described general chatbot or a fixed set of supplied examples. The formal post-test AI-access protocol is not stated (PDF pp. 6 and 11-12).

task.description: Create and develop original music compositions, including melody, harmony, multi-section musical form, and integration of Guangdong musical traditions; final composition portfolios receive expert evaluation (PDF p. 9, Table 2; pp. 11-12, Table 4; p. 20, Table 7).
task.duration: Described as a 12-week intervention (PDF p. 5, Sec. 3.1; p. 8, Sec. 4.1). Figure 1 places baseline at week 0, intervention in weeks 1-12, and assessment in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 5); Table 4 instead places preparation in weeks 1-2, modules in weeks 3-12, and synthesis/evaluation in weeks 13-14 (PDF pp. 11-12). Per-composition time limit not stated.

outcomes.name: Overall Creativity
outcomes.measure_detail: Compositional Product Assessment Rubric (CPAR) scores on musical compositions, ranging from 1 (lowest) to 5 (highest), assessed by five expert evaluators (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; p. 14, Table 5 note; p. 17, Sec. 5.3; p. 20, Table 7 note). Direct expert rating of overall creativity; first under the codebook hierarchy, although the paper designates no primary outcome. Pre-test, post-test, and change scores are repeated measurements of this outcome; Figures 2-4 repeat these dimensions. Tables 5-6 report group n=60 and describe students' compositional ability, whereas Figure 6 separately counts 120 compositions (PDF pp. 12-15 and 22). The paper does not specify whether the dimensional analyses use one composition per student or a participant score aggregated across portfolio pieces, nor explicitly map them to the Figure 6 corpus. Unit and n_units therefore remain null for those dimensional analyses; the people count remains 120. Classroom AI use and selected AI-assisted examples are documented, but the production/access protocol for the main post-test outputs is unspecified (PDF pp. 6, 9, 11-12 and 18). Neither continued access nor AI removal is assumed; question and ai_available_when_produced remain null.
outcomes.delay: Figure 1 places intervention in weeks 1-12 and assessment in weeks 13-14 (PDF p. 5); Table 4 places preparation in weeks 1-2 and final composition development/evaluation in weeks 13-14 (PDF pp. 11-12). The interval and session schedule between final AI use, production, and assessment are not given. Immediate versus delayed cannot be confirmed; no delay in days is inferred.

eligibility.reason: S1 meets all three criteria on the reported design. Figure 1 explicitly labels group division Randomized Assignment to AI-assisted composition versus traditional instruction (PDF p. 5, printed p. 2794), and the paragraph after Table 1 states that a randomization procedure created comparable groups (PDF p. 7, printed p. 2796). AICP integrates generative artificial neural networks and supports students' own music compositions (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; p. 9, Table 2). The study reports 120 randomized students, 60 per arm (PDF p. 5, Figure 1), and 120 analyzed students, 60 per arm (PDF p. 7, Table 1; pp. 13 and 15, Tables 5-6), meeting the people threshold without the separate pilot. Experts assessed the produced compositions on originality and overall creativity, among other dimensions (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; p. 17, Sec. 5.3; p. 20, Table 7 note). The conflicting quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 1 and 5-6) and unspecified allocation method remain an eligibility-relevant author query for criterion 1; the explicit randomization claims support met as reported. Post-test AI availability, timing, and the dimensional analysis unit remain unspecified; these limit question classification and extraction, rather than negate the reported randomization, analyzed people count, or output scoring. Figure 6 disagrees with its accompanying rank-count prose (PDF p. 22), and the entropy-weight calculation needs clarification (PDF p. 21, Table 9). Those issues concern the composite results, not the existence of eligible output outcomes. Table 7 contains selected examples, not a separate sample or full-sample treatment effect.

one_line_finding: Among 120 analyzed music students, post-test overall creativity was 4.71 (SD 0.54) after the AI-assisted curriculum versus 3.62 (SD 0.69) after traditional instruction, with reported Cohen's d=1.77 and p<.001; AI access during the main post-test work is unspecified (PDF p. 15, Table 6; pp. 6 and 11-12, methods).
open_questions: How was the randomized assignment implemented, and were students allocated individually or through institutional/classroom units? The field_rct/individual coding follows the student flowchart and explicit randomization statement, but the method is unspecified and conflicts with the quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 5-7).

Were the main post-test outputs in Tables 5-6 and Figure 6 produced with AICP available or after removal? The explicitly AI-assisted selected Table 7 examples do not establish access for every main outcome (PDF pp. 6, 9, 11-12, 18 and 20-22).

What was the interval between the final AI-assisted activity, production of assessed compositions, and the post-test? Figure 1 and Table 4 place evaluation in weeks 13-14 but do not give that interval; their preparation/intervention schedules also differ (PDF p. 5 and pp. 11-12).

Does each observation in Tables 5-6 represent a participant aggregate or an individual composition, and how does it map to the 120 compositions ranked in Figure 6? Rater/portfolio aggregation and the participant-to-output mapping are not specified (PDF pp. 6, 12-15 and 20-22).

Which rank counts are correct: the labels inside Figure 6 or the different counts in its accompanying prose? The threshold counts are also provided only in the prose, without underlying data (PDF pp. 22-23).

How were the entropy weights normalized and the comprehensive score calculated? The listed proportions do not form a normalized percentage distribution, and no full calculation or underlying scores is supplied (PDF p. 21, Table 9; pp. 22-23, Sec. 5.5).

What are the detailed CPAR anchors, particularly the Creative Fluency and Expressive Range dimensions? The paper supplies expert ratings but no idea or category counts; rater blinding is not stated (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; pp. 13-15; p. 20, Table 7).

Are separate Creativity Assessment Battery subtest results or the stated MANCOVA results available? CAB musical divergent thinking, compositional flexibility, and creative originality are named in methods, but separate results and output-scoring details are not provided; MANCOVA is stated without a results table or coefficients (PDF pp. 6-7, Secs. 3.2 and 3.4; results on pp. 12-23). No supplement is referenced.

CAB subtests lack separately identifiable output scores, and the separate 28-student instrument pilot has no reported intervention comparison. Table 10 correlations are ancillary evidence. open_items.item: open_questions[0]: How was the randomized assignment implemented, and were students allocated individually or through institutional/classroom units? The field_rct/individual coding follows the student flowchart and explicit randomization statement, but the method is unspecified and conflicts with the quasi-experimental label (PDF pp. 5-7). This concerns criterion 1: the explicit randomization claims support the present met decision, but author confirmation of the allocation procedure and unit, and an explanation of the quasi-experimental label, would settle the conflict. Non-random allocation would change eligibility; the exact clustering unit alone concerns analysis and precision.

open_questions[1]: Were the main post-test outputs in Tables 5-6 and Figure 6 produced with AICP available or after removal? The explicitly AI-assisted selected Table 7 examples do not establish access for every main outcome (PDF pp. 6, 9, 11-12, 18 and 20-22). Also covers reconciliation.differences[1] (question) and [2] (ai_available_when_produced). The authors must supply the production instructions and AI-access rule for the main scored outputs. This determines with_ai versus after_ai; both questions are within scope, so none of the three eligibility criteria depends on this distinction.

open_questions[2]: What was the interval between the final AI-assisted activity, production of assessed compositions, and the post-test? Figure 1 and Table 4 place evaluation in weeks 13-14 but do not give that interval; their preparation/intervention schedules also differ (PDF p. 5 and pp. 11-12). Also covers reconciliation.differences[3] (timing_and_delay), including the selected-example outcome. The authors must provide the session schedule or dates linking final AI use, output production, and evaluation and reconcile Figure 1 with Table 4. This affects timing and delay coding, not an eligibility criterion.

open_questions[3]: Does each observation in Tables 5-6 represent a participant aggregate or an individual composition, and how does it map to the 120 compositions ranked in Figure 6? Rater/portfolio aggregation and the participant-to-output mapping are not specified (PDF pp. 6, 12-15 and 20-22). Also covers reconciliation.differences[4] (unit) and [5] (n_units). The authors must supply the participant-to-composition mapping and the rater/portfolio aggregation rules used in Tables 5-6 and Figure 6. This affects the observation count, standardizer, and precision for extraction; Tables 5-6 independently report 60 analyzed people per arm, and expert scoring of compositions is established, so criteria 2 and 3 remain met.

open_questions[4]: Which rank counts are correct: the labels inside Figure 6 or the different counts in its accompanying prose? The threshold counts are also provided only in the prose, without underlying data (PDF pp. 22-23). Also covers the source discrepancy retained in reconciliation.differences[16]. The authors must identify the correct Figure 6 rank-block counts and verify the threshold summaries, supported by composition scores and group labels. The saved figure and prose cannot settle their disagreement. This affects the composite contrast, not the analyzed people count or the existence of output scoring.

open_questions[5]: How were the entropy weights normalized and the comprehensive score calculated? The listed proportions do not form a normalized percentage distribution, and no full calculation or underlying scores is supplied (PDF p. 21, Table 9; pp. 22-23, Sec. 5.5). Also covers the methodological uncertainty retained in reconciliation.differences[15]. The authors must provide the entropy-weight normalization and comprehensive-score formula or calculation code, with any correction to Table 9. Printed weights are retained. This affects the composite measure, not an eligibility criterion; the directly rated creativity dimensions separately establish criterion 3.

open_questions[6]: What are the detailed CPAR anchors, particularly the Creative Fluency and Expressive Range dimensions? The paper supplies expert ratings but no idea or category counts; rater blinding is not stated (PDF p. 6, Sec. 3.2; pp. 13-15; p. 20, Table 7). The authors must provide the CPAR scoring anchors and rater instructions, including whether evaluators were blinded. These details could refine construct coding and assessment of bias. Existing expert ratings of originality and overall creativity on compositions already meet criterion 3; idea counts are not required for that decision.

open_questions[7]: Are separate Creativity Assessment Battery subtest results or the stated MANCOVA results available? CAB musical divergent thinking, compositional flexibility, and creative originality are named in methods, but separate results and output-scoring details are not provided; MANCOVA is stated without a results table or coefficients (PDF pp. 6-7, Secs. 3.2 and 3.4; results on pp. 12-23). No supplement is referenced. The authors must supply the separate CAB output-scoring protocols/results and the stated MANCOVA coefficients or results table, or confirm they are unavailable. No supplement or data/code source is identified in the saved journal article. These materials could expand the outcome inventory and extraction, but the reported CPAR outcomes already meet criterion 3.
